author: John Naisbitt
title: Megatrends: Ten New Directions Transforming Our Lives
summary: Naisbitt read local news for signs that Americans were changing how they worked, lived and organised. He presented ten paired shifts. Their geography matters, especially in his account of Americans moving south and west.

trends.name: From factories to information work
trends.detail: Creating, handling and circulating information were becoming central economic activities.

trends.name: High tech, high touch
trends.detail: As machines entered more settings, people would seek personal attention, human contact and opportunities to participate.

trends.name: National economies become interdependent
trends.detail: US firms and workers increasingly faced decisions shaped by trade, investment and production abroad.

trends.name: Planning beyond the next quarter
trends.detail: The book anticipated more attention to the longer consequences of decisions in business and public life.

trends.name: Decisions move closer to communities
trends.detail: States, towns and local initiatives would gain influence as large central institutions lost authority.

trends.name: From institutional provision to self-help
trends.detail: People would organise around shared needs and take more responsibility for their own welfare.

trends.name: Citizens seek a direct say
trends.detail: Voting for representatives would sit alongside participation in decisions affecting workplaces and communities.

trends.name: Networks challenge hierarchies
trends.detail: People could share information across organisational boundaries and coordinate through informal relationships.

trends.name: The American Sun Belt gains weight
trends.detail: Population and business shifted from the US industrial North towards southern and western states. This was a domestic shift.

trends.name: More ways to live
trends.detail: Mass markets and binary social choices gave way to a wider range of careers, products and lifestyles.

author: John Naisbitt and Patricia Aburdene
title: Megatrends 2000: Ten New Directions for the 1990s
summary: Published in 1990, the sequel widened its geographical reach. The authors connected economic integration with surprising cultural responses, including renewed attachment to national identity and religion.

trends.name: A decade of worldwide economic expansion
trends.detail: The authors expected a long global upswing as markets opened and commerce crossed borders.

trends.name: An arts revival
trends.detail: They expected attendance, investment and participation in the arts to expand.

trends.name: Socialism adopts market mechanisms
trends.detail: Market reforms in socialist economies suggested possible combinations of public goals and price signals.

trends.name: Global lifestyles and cultural belonging
trends.detail: Shared consumer habits could grow alongside stronger assertions of national languages and traditions.

trends.name: Welfare provision shifts to private hands
trends.detail: Governments would transfer some responsibility for public services and social protection to other providers.

trends.name: The Pacific becomes an economic centre
trends.detail: Trade and economic dynamism around the Pacific would redraw the map of opportunity.

trends.name: Women gain leadership roles
trends.detail: Women would take on greater authority in organisations, enterprise and politics.

trends.name: Biology becomes a defining science
trends.detail: Biotechnology would create business opportunities and bring choices about living systems into public debate.

trends.name: Religion gains influence
trends.detail: The approach of the millennium would stimulate spiritual searching across established and newer religious movements.

trends.name: Individuals gain agency
trends.detail: Personal initiative and choice would gain influence over institutions and collective orthodoxies.

author: Patricia Aburdene and John Naisbitt
title: Megatrends for Women
summary: The authors turned a single 1990 heading into a book on changing institutions. They also predicted a woman would be US president by 2004. That missed deadline illustrates the distance between identifying a direction and timing a particular event. These are themes highlighted in the publisher’s description.

trends.name: Electoral representation
trends.detail: The authors read growing numbers of women standing for office as a sign that the presidency could soon follow.

trends.name: Enterprise and management
trends.detail: Women building businesses and leading workplaces were changing who held economic authority and how management was practised.

trends.name: Civic leadership
trends.detail: Organising around housing, public safety and the environment gave women a route to shaping public priorities.

trends.name: Sport and fitness
trends.detail: Participation in everyday sport and success in elite competition challenged assumptions about who belonged in athletics.

trends.name: Health and medical research
trends.detail: Women’s advocacy around ageing, heart disease and breast cancer could reshape clinical and research priorities.

trends.name: Religious authority
trends.detail: Women leaders and theologians questioned inherited accounts of spiritual authority and divinity.

trends.name: Fashion and cultural production
trends.detail: Women designers assumed authority in an industry whose senior creative roles often went to men.

trends.name: Politics after the Cold War
trends.detail: The authors thought domestic issues would command more attention, opening new opportunities for women in public leadership.

author: John Naisbitt
title: Megatrends Asia
summary: Naisbitt asked how growth driven within Asia might change the global economy. He put business networks with links to Chinese diaspora communities at the centre of his account. His eight shifts generalised across very different countries.

trends.name: Business networks cross national borders
trends.detail: Family, commercial and diaspora relationships linked economic activity across several jurisdictions.

trends.name: Domestic consumers drive demand
trends.detail: Household spending within Asian markets would become a stronger engine of growth alongside exports.

trends.name: Modernisation on Asian terms
trends.detail: Prosperity could strengthen local cultural identities and development models.

trends.name: Markets gain influence over investment
trends.detail: The author expected private enterprise to gain scope in economies shaped by government direction.

trends.name: Growth concentrates in large cities
trends.detail: Migration and investment would transform previously rural societies and enlarge metropolitan centres.

trends.name: Industry moves into advanced technology
trends.detail: Manufacturers could move beyond labour-intensive production into higher-value goods and capabilities.

trends.name: Women gain economic influence
trends.detail: Changing employment and business opportunities would challenge male control of leadership positions.

trends.name: The world’s economic centre shifts east
trends.detail: Asian economies together would reshape patterns of global opportunity and influence.

author: US National Intelligence Council
title: Mapping the Global Future
summary: The Council consulted experts internationally and explored four alternative futures. It treated globalisation as a force shaping the other developments, while asking who would benefit and where it might provoke resistance. The entries below are its four principal analytical themes.

trends.name: The uneven gains of globalisation
trends.detail: Faster flows of capital, labour and technology could create wealth while unsettling jobs and intensifying domestic political tensions.

trends.name: New powers, especially China and India
trends.detail: The relative rise of large Asian economies could change alliances, energy demand and the position of the United States.

trends.name: Governance struggles to keep pace
trends.detail: Democratic change, identity politics and international institutions’ ability to manage cross-border problems could diverge.

trends.name: Persistent insecurity
trends.detail: Conflict, terrorism and fear could remain politically potent even if many people became more prosperous.

author: Patricia Aburdene
title: Megatrends 2010: The Rise of Conscious Capitalism
summary: Aburdene brought the 1990 themes of individual agency and spiritual revival into the workplace. Her seven substantive chapters asked whether managers, consumers and investors could change the purposes companies serve.

trends.name: Personal spirituality influences organisations
trends.detail: The search for meaning in individuals’ working lives could shape the cultures of entire organisations.

trends.name: Business takes wider responsibilities
trends.detail: Companies would increasingly consider employees, communities and environmental impacts when defining success.

trends.name: Middle managers lead change
trends.detail: People with limited formal authority could shift company behaviour through everyday management decisions.

trends.name: Faith and reflection enter working life
trends.detail: Employees and managers were making space for spiritual practices and discussion at work.

trends.name: Purchases express values
trends.detail: Some customers would choose goods according to a producer’s social and environmental conduct.

trends.name: Conscious practices become management tools
trends.detail: The book considered ways firms could apply reflective practices to workplace problems and examine the results.

trends.name: Investment incorporates social criteria
trends.detail: Investors could direct capital towards firms that met ethical or environmental standards.

author: US National Intelligence Council
title: Global Trends 2025: A Transformed World
summary: The Council moved multipolarity closer to the centre of its outlook and explored four alternative futures. Its seven analytical chapters already put demographic divergence, resource insecurity and the politics of interdependence on the agenda.

trends.name: The world economy gains new centres
trends.detail: Growth in Asia, a larger middle class and state-led capitalist models could change where wealth accumulated and who set the rules.

trends.name: Age structures pull countries apart
trends.detail: Some populations would shrink and age while others retained large younger cohorts. Migration and urbanisation could change the consequences.

trends.name: More states gain international influence
trends.detail: China, India and other rising powers would have greater capacity to shape regional and global decisions.

trends.name: Resources grow more contested
trends.detail: Energy transitions, demand for water and food, and climate stress could shift the balance between importers and exporters.

trends.name: New pressures for conflict
trends.detail: Resource competition, instability and the spread of military capabilities could strain relations within and between states.

trends.name: Global institutions face harder problems
trends.detail: More centres of power could make cooperation harder even as transnational networks gained influence.

trends.name: US leadership requires power sharing
trends.detail: A still powerful United States could face tighter constraints and greater reliance on partners.

author: CSIRO Futures
title: Our Future World
summary: Australia’s national science agency revised its 2010 draft after feedback from researchers, businesses and communities. Looking towards 2032 from Australia changes the geography of the story. Rising incomes in Asia mean new tourists, investors and intellectual exchange as well as new markets.

trends.name: More from less
trends.detail: Growing demand puts pressure on water, food, energy and minerals. Efficiency and changes in consumption could stretch supplies.

trends.name: Going, going … gone?
trends.detail: Habitat and species loss can become permanent. The question mark leaves room for conservation to alter the outcome.

trends.name: The silk highway
trends.detail: Asian growth redirects trade, capital, tourism and ideas, reshaping Australia’s relationships with its neighbours.

trends.name: Forever young
trends.detail: Older populations bring accumulated skills and experience as well as new demands on care, pensions and employment.

trends.name: Virtually here
trends.detail: Shopping, public services, work and relationships increasingly take place online.

trends.name: Great expectations
trends.detail: Consumers seek personalised services and memorable experiences. Relationships can matter more than acquiring another possession.

author: KPMG International and the Mowat Centre
title: Future State 2030
summary: The 2013 study asked what nine global changes would mean for national governments. Public borrowing earns a place alongside climate and demography because a government’s ability to finance services shapes how citizens experience those changes.

trends.name: Population structure
trends.detail: Some governments face pension and care pressures while others must create jobs for large younger cohorts.

trends.name: Individual empowerment
trends.detail: Better education, health and communications raise expectations of participation and transparency.

trends.name: Technology as an enabler
trends.detail: New tools expand what governments can deliver while creating difficult regulatory choices.

trends.name: Economic interdependence
trends.detail: Cross-border trade and investment spread both economic gains and financial shocks.

trends.name: Public debt
trends.detail: Servicing debt can squeeze the resources available for future public services.

trends.name: Shifting economic power
trends.detail: Emerging economies gain bargaining power over the rules of trade and investment.

trends.name: Climate change
trends.detail: Governments face decisions about cutting emissions, adapting infrastructure and sharing the costs.

trends.name: Strains on resources
trends.detail: Demand for water, energy and food puts competing users into closer contact.

trends.name: Urban growth
trends.detail: Fast-growing cities must fund housing, transport and services at the pace of settlement.

author: PwC
title: Five Global Megatrends
summary: Five members of PwC’s network leadership each picked a force likely to matter to clients over the following decade. The short list offered businesses a shared vocabulary. Demographic divergence was already explicit in its first item.

trends.name: Population shifts
trends.detail: Workforces and demand for services diverge between countries with rapid ageing and countries with youthful growth.

trends.name: Economic power moves
trends.detail: Emerging economies gain weight as markets and sources of investment.

trends.name: Faster urbanisation
trends.detail: More economic activity concentrates in cities, increasing demand for infrastructure.

trends.name: Climate and resource pressures
trends.detail: Growing demand for food, water and energy coincides with climatic disruption.

trends.name: Technological breakthroughs
trends.detail: Digital tools alter products, business models and the speed of competition.

author: OECD
title: Science, Technology and Innovation Outlook 2016
summary: Chapter one groups the forces bearing on research and innovation into eight themes, with a typical horizon of 10–15 years. The relationship works in both directions. Ageing can steer research towards care technologies, while new treatments can change what an ageing population needs.

trends.name: Population change
trends.detail: Ageing, growth and migration reshape the supply of skills and the needs research addresses.

trends.name: Energy and natural resources
trends.detail: Food, water and energy pressures make efficiency and alternative supplies research priorities.

trends.name: Climate and ecosystems
trends.detail: Environmental damage creates demand for cleaner technologies and adaptation.

trends.name: Global integration
trends.detail: Knowledge, investment and research cross borders. Countries can collaborate while competing for their benefits.

trends.name: Government’s evolving role
trends.detail: Public funding, regulation and international cooperation help determine which innovations reach people.

trends.name: Employment and productivity
trends.detail: Changes in growth, skills and automation raise questions about jobs and how productivity gains are shared.

trends.name: Social change
trends.detail: Urban growth, education and shifting expectations alter who participates in innovation.

trends.name: Health and unequal well-being
trends.detail: Disease burdens and unequal access influence medical priorities and who benefits from advances.

author: European Commission Joint Research Centre
title: Megatrends Hub
summary: Development began in 2016 and the public Hub opened in 2018. Its fourteen forces are global, selected for their relevance to Europe. The launch booklet emphasised the changing forms of inequality and the spread of consumerism. Later Hub entries also emphasise widening inequalities and growing consumption.

trends.name: More connected technologies
trends.detail: Digital networks connect work, government, production and social life.

trends.name: Pressure on resources
trends.detail: Demand intensifies competition for land, water, energy and materials.

trends.name: Changing work
trends.detail: Automation and new business models alter occupations and working conditions.

trends.name: New security threats
trends.detail: Threats arise from a wider range of actors and extend across borders.

trends.name: Climate and ecosystem damage
trends.detail: Warming, pollution and biodiversity loss change the conditions societies depend on.

trends.name: Continuing urbanisation
trends.detail: Cities gain people and influence, widening demands on services.

trends.name: More ways to learn
trends.detail: Learning stretches across a lifetime, through more providers and channels.

trends.name: Changing inequalities
trends.detail: Disadvantage takes different forms across places, generations and social groups.

trends.name: Influence moves east and south
trends.detail: Emerging economies gain influence over global affairs.

trends.name: Growing consumer culture
trends.detail: Rising purchasing power changes demand and environmental footprints.

trends.name: Diverging populations
trends.detail: Growth, ageing and shrinking populations coexist across regions.

trends.name: New forms of governance
trends.detail: Cities, networks and other actors share influence with national authorities.

trends.name: Migration’s growing significance
trends.detail: Cross-border movement becomes more consequential for economies and politics.

trends.name: Changing health burdens
trends.detail: Lifestyle, ageing and environmental exposures reshape health needs.

author: Filippo Artuso and Irene Guijt, Oxfam
title: Global Megatrends: Mapping the Forces that Affect Us All
summary: The authors compared 22 scans and organised their findings into four clusters. For organisations tackling poverty, they asked whose experience broad labels conceal. Gender, civic freedoms and the causes of conflict received too little attention in the underlying literature.

trends.name: Technological innovation
trends.detail: Automation can improve services and concentrate gains among technology owners.

trends.name: Hyperconnectivity
trends.detail: Networks speed communication, commerce and surveillance.

trends.name: Changing work
trends.detail: Platform work can increase flexibility and expose workers to insecurity.

trends.name: Age structures
trends.detail: Youthful populations need employment opportunities. Older populations change care needs.

trends.name: Urbanisation
trends.detail: Fast-growing settlements may outpace water, housing and transport provision.

trends.name: Migration
trends.detail: Movement creates opportunities while exposing some migrants to exploitation.

trends.name: Health challenges
trends.detail: New treatments, mobility and population ageing reshape disease burdens.

trends.name: Climate change
trends.detail: Heat, flooding and disrupted livelihoods affect groups with different means to adapt.

trends.name: Resource scarcity
trends.detail: Unequal access to water, food and energy compounds hardship.

trends.name: Multipolarity
trends.detail: New centres of economic and political influence contest existing rules.

trends.name: Economic inequality
trends.detail: Gaps in income and wealth persist within and across countries.

trends.name: Conflict
trends.detail: Interacting political and resource pressures can increase insecurity.

trends.name: Weakening social cohesion
trends.detail: Polarisation and institutional distrust make collective decisions harder.

author: United Nations Economist Network
title: Shaping the Trends of Our Time
summary: Five forces form a test of progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals. The UN economists ask how policy can change their direction and who shares in their benefits.

trends.name: Climate change
trends.detail: Emissions, exposure and the ability to adapt connect development choices to future losses.

trends.name: Demographic change
trends.detail: Longer lives and changing fertility reshape the age mix, demand for care and opportunities for work.

trends.name: Urbanisation
trends.detail: The location and design of settlement determine access to jobs, transport, housing and services.

trends.name: Digital technologies
trends.detail: Connectivity opens access to services and markets while unequal access can widen existing divides.

trends.name: Inequalities
trends.detail: Disparities within and between countries shape who can use new opportunities or absorb shocks.

author: EY
title: Megatrends 2020 and beyond
summary: EY traces eight developments to human augmentation, changing globalisation, Generation Z and intensifying climate impacts. Its longer-range questions concern Africa’s influence, measures of economic progress and repairing social ties.

trends.name: Decarbonising the economy
trends.detail: Lower-carbon production changes what businesses buy, sell and invest in.

trends.name: Technology rivalry
trends.detail: Strategic competition can split markets, supply chains and technical standards.

trends.name: Markets shaped by behaviour
trends.detail: Data and behavioural science increase organisations’ ability to influence everyday choices.

trends.name: Machine-made media
trends.detail: Synthetic images, voices and text complicate the work of establishing authenticity.

trends.name: Changes in how people think
trends.detail: Digital tools redistribute attention, memory and judgement between people and machines.

trends.name: Work crossing into home life
trends.detail: Digital access erodes boundaries of workplace, hours and employment arrangements.

trends.name: Microbial communities
trends.detail: Research into microbiomes opens questions for medicine, agriculture and consumer products.

trends.name: Biology as a design medium
trends.detail: Biological production offers new ways to make medicines, materials and other goods.

author: CSIRO
title: Our Future World
summary: CSIRO revisited its 2012 study with a horizon of 2042. The new edition gives separate treatment to climate adaptation, health and machine autonomy. Its intended users span Australian communities, businesses and government.

trends.name: Living with climate change
trends.detail: Hotter conditions and extreme events change the design of homes, infrastructure and emergency services.

trends.name: Using resources more efficiently
trends.detail: Cleaner energy and circular production respond to material limits and waste.

trends.name: Rising health pressures
trends.detail: Pandemic threats and the long-term burden of illness both demand preparedness.

trends.name: Shifting geopolitical power
trends.detail: Trade, security and supply decisions respond to changing alliances and strategic competition.

trends.name: Wider digital adoption
trends.detail: Digital services reach further into work, education, care and trade.

trends.name: Greater machine autonomy
trends.detail: AI and robotics can perform a growing range of tasks with less direct supervision.

trends.name: Human needs and trust
trends.detail: Inclusion, transparency and public confidence influence which innovations find acceptance.

author: Andthen for the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
title: Global Megatrends 2024
summary: The fourth edition gives each force a proposed historical starting point and a confidence judgement. It traces urban settlement and environmental degradation back to early agriculture, and species-wide technological risk to 1945. These dates express the authors’ interpretation of when a process began.

trends.name: More volatile geopolitics
trends.detail: Industrialisation intensifies international competition over resources and influence.

trends.name: Growing risks to humanity
trends.detail: Technological capabilities create hazards capable of affecting civilisation on a global scale.

trends.name: Accelerating human-caused warming
trends.detail: Fossil fuel use drives changes that compound across generations.

trends.name: Accelerating environmental damage
trends.detail: Land use, pollution and biodiversity loss have long histories, with faster recent change.

trends.name: Scarcity and shifting competition
trends.detail: Resource demand changes bargaining power between suppliers and users.

trends.name: Changing demography
trends.detail: Mortality and fertility transitions produce contrasting age structures.

trends.name: Fraying social ties
trends.detail: Polarisation and distrust strain institutions that support collective action.

trends.name: Urban concentration
trends.detail: Centuries of settlement growth concentrate people, infrastructure and exposure.

trends.name: Science as a worldview
trends.detail: Scientific explanation and technological solutions increasingly organise decisions.

trends.name: Pursuit of economic growth
trends.detail: Governments and firms continue to organise activity around expanding output.

author: Claire Naughtin, Emma Schleiger, Alexandra Bratanova, Andrew Terhorst and Stefan Hajkowicz
title: Forty Years in the Making
summary: This review examined 267 academic and practitioner publications from 1982–2022. It found considerable variation in definitions and methods. Its contribution is a way to test a candidate’s breadth, duration, influence across domains and relevance to future change, and a process for developing and validating claims. A repeated label across reports may trace back to a common source.

author: UN DESA Population Division
title: World Population Prospects 2024
summary: An empirical check on demographic divergence. The UN groups 237 countries and areas by the timing of their population peak. The future groups describe projections subject to assumptions about fertility, mortality and migration.

trends.name: Already past peak population
trends.detail: By 2024, the population had already peaked in 63 countries and areas, including China, Germany and Japan.

trends.name: Projected to peak within three decades
trends.detail: The UN projects a peak between 2025 and 2054 for 48 countries and areas, including Brazil, Iran and Viet Nam.

trends.name: Projected to grow through 2054
trends.detail: The other 126, including India, Nigeria and the United States, are expected to keep growing through 2054. The contribution of migration varies.

author: Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies
title: Megatrends 2026
summary: The institute tests candidate trends against duration, direction and structural reach. Its eleven selections make infrastructure ownership, wealth concentration and limits on economic growth visible alongside older themes.

trends.name: A multipolar world
trends.detail: China and middle powers challenge sole US leadership over international rules.

trends.name: Age structures turn upside down
trends.detail: Fertility falls and lifespans lengthen at different speeds across countries.

trends.name: The green transition
trends.detail: Clean power expands while reducing material use and protecting habitats prove harder.

trends.name: More individual life paths
trends.detail: Households shrink and life stages become more flexible, sometimes increasing loneliness.

trends.name: Health beyond treatment
trends.detail: Chronic conditions and everyday environments make care a continuing concern.

trends.name: AI built into infrastructure
trends.detail: AI becomes harder to opt out of as organisations embed it in services.

trends.name: Biotechnology across sectors
trends.detail: Biological advances expand options in healthcare, agriculture and manufacturing.

trends.name: More constrained economies
trends.detail: Conditions that supported post-Cold War integration and growth weaken.

trends.name: New patterns of urban growth
trends.detail: Rapid growth in Asian and African cities stretches institutions and services.

trends.name: Authority through networks
trends.detail: Operators of cross-border digital systems gain influence over essential functions.

trends.name: Concentrated wealth
trends.detail: Accumulated assets give their owners an outsized share of growth and influence.

author: Sitra
title: Megatrends 2026. Towards a new social contract
summary: Sitra interprets global forces from Finland’s position as an ageing welfare state. A renewed social contract is its proposal for sharing rights, costs and responsibilities across the four trajectories.

trends.name: Building a society for longer lives
trends.detail: Low fertility, migration and longevity create demand for lifelong learning, care and new forms of community.

trends.name: Democracy under geopolitical pressure
trends.detail: Finland’s response to a shifting world order depends partly on credible information and opportunities to participate.

trends.name: Adapting to ecological crisis
trends.detail: Climate and biodiversity pressures prompt choices about energy, material reuse and restoring nature.

trends.name: AI enters society’s core institutions
trends.detail: Research, education and public decisions face new questions about evidence, productivity and accountability.

author: EY
title: Futures Reimagined. Megatrends 2026 and beyond
summary: EY places eight developments in three sets concerning human–machine work, access to scarce resources and the economic order. The comparison with its 2020 report brings talent, trust and capital allocation into focus.

trends.name: Companies reorganised around automation
trends.detail: Agents may change how work moves across departments and who approves decisions.

trends.name: Human–machine collaboration
trends.detail: AI, robotics and other tools can extend what workers can do.

trends.name: Measuring productivity again
trends.detail: Output volume alone says little about the quality of a decision or an idea.

trends.name: Developing people and AI together
trends.detail: Workforce planning must account for learning by both staff and machines.

trends.name: Migration as economic infrastructure
trends.detail: Recruitment, housing and settlement affect whether migration eases labour shortages.

trends.name: Competition for resources
trends.detail: Access to energy, materials and emerging resource frontiers becomes strategically important.

trends.name: The economic value of trust
trends.detail: Confidence in institutions, information and firms can influence where people transact.

trends.name: Rebalancing capitalism
trends.detail: Long-term investment in people, resilience and nature can compete with near-term financial rewards.

author: World Economic Forum
title: The Global Risks Report 2026
summary: The survey measures expected severity. Four underlying structural forces, first identified in the 2024 edition, help explain why respondents rank risks differently over two and ten years. The two lists below are in rank order.

trends.name: Faster technological change
trends.detail: New capabilities spread opportunities and vulnerabilities across systems.

trends.name: Changing geopolitical power
trends.detail: Rivalries and contested alliances alter who sets the rules.

trends.name: A changing climate
trends.detail: Warming alters physical systems and the hazards societies face.

trends.name: Diverging populations
trends.detail: Differences in population growth and age structure widen.

trends.name: Two-year risk ranking
trends.detail: 1 economic confrontation, 2 false information, 3 polarisation, 4 extreme weather, 5 armed conflict involving states, 6 digital insecurity, 7 inequality, 8 loss of rights and civic freedoms, 9 pollution, 10 forced movement.

trends.name: Ten-year risk ranking
trends.detail: 1 extreme weather, 2 biodiversity and ecosystem loss, 3 major Earth-system changes, 4 false information, 5 AI harms, 6 resource shortages, 7 inequality, 8 digital insecurity, 9 polarisation, 10 pollution.

author: McKinsey & Company
title: Technology Trends Outlook 2026
summary: The sixth edition compares 14 domains using indicators including patents, research, investment and hiring. Software agents and AI-assisted scientific discovery enter as separate domains. Investment measures activity and cannot establish eventual societal effects.

trends.name: AI infrastructure and models
trends.detail: Chips, data centres and model architecture jointly shape capacity.

trends.name: Agents for multi-step work
trends.detail: Systems take actions across tools with varying supervision.

trends.name: Software development with agents
trends.detail: Agents increasingly draft, test and revise software.

trends.name: AI in science and engineering
trends.detail: Computation helps researchers propose candidates and explore designs.

trends.name: Advanced connectivity
trends.detail: Communications networks expand bandwidth and coverage.

trends.name: Specialised semiconductors
trends.detail: Purpose-built chips optimise particular computing workloads.

trends.name: Cybersecurity and trusted systems
trends.detail: Organisations need dependable protection as digital dependencies grow.

trends.name: Quantum technologies
trends.detail: Computing, sensing and communications develop at different speeds.

trends.name: Immersive interfaces
trends.detail: Spatial displays and wearables connect physical and digital environments.

trends.name: Robotics
trends.detail: Machines gain perception and flexibility in physical settings.

trends.name: New mobility technologies
trends.detail: Autonomous systems and electrification reshape transport options.

trends.name: Life sciences and bioengineering
trends.detail: Advances in diagnostics and therapies change healthcare possibilities.

trends.name: Space technologies
trends.detail: Launch, satellite services and orbital operations attract investment.

trends.name: Energy and sustainability technologies
trends.detail: Grids, storage and generation influence industrial and computing capacity.
